feat(notifications): add the Telegram channel

<!-- synapse-epic:external-integrations:C02:v1 -->

Part of #1331 (WS3) in EPIC #1327. **Priority:** P0a. **Key:** `C02`.

## Goal

Deliver every event to Telegram with built-in templates and safe formatting.

## To do

- [ ] Channel type, sealed per-type config and validation (Bot API `sendMessage` on `api.telegram.org`, bot token and chat ID, optional `message_thread_id`).
- [ ] Driver behind the registry; formatter and escaper from T02.
- [ ] Console form: create, edit (re-enter the full URL or token), test, delete; data class selector.
- [ ] The full credential-bearing URL is sealed; the UI shows `scheme://host/…` only; transport errors are never wrapped into logged or persisted strings.
- [ ] Docs in `docs/guide/notifications.md`, CHANGELOG entry.
- [ ] MarkdownV2 escaping of every value.

## How

- Register in `cmd/synapse-worker/main.go` and the API catalog.
- Fake-server contract test; dial-error test proving the token is absent from logs, attempt rows and API responses.

## Expected output when this issue closes

- Telegram channel usable end to end from the console.

## Acceptance tests

- [ ] Contract test for success, 4xx, 429 with `Retry-After`, 5xx.
- [ ] Escaping vectors for the channel.
- [ ] Token leak test.

## Evidence required

Screenshots from the real client(s): **Telegram**, showing at least these messages delivered through this channel:
1. a critical `finding.created` (or `vulnerability_action.created` if WS1 slice 1 is not merged yet);
2. an enriched `scan.completed` with new and fixed counts;
3. `sla.approaching_deadline`;
4. `incident.created`;
5. a message whose finding title contains `[Reset password](https://evil.example)`, `@everyone`, `<!channel>` and `**bold**`, proving it renders as literal text.

Each in English and Vietnamese, in the client's light and dark theme where supported, on desktop and on mobile (one screenshot per client from the mobile app or a narrow browser).

Every screenshot is read by the reviewer before approval. It must show:
- the rendered message, not raw Markdown, HTML entities, `<no value>` or escaped tags;
- the severity label and color, the title and the key facts expected for the destination's data class;
- a deep link whose host is `SYNAPSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, and clicking it opens the right console page;
- Vietnamese text with intact diacritics for the `vi` locale;
- no token, webhook URL, routing key, password or secret value anywhere in the frame (mask the channel settings).

Screenshots go in the PR description (drag and drop), grouped by client and locale, named `<client>-<event>-<locale>-<theme>.png`. Use dedicated test workspaces, never a customer or production channel.

Console screenshots of every new or changed screen in light and dark theme, including loading, empty, error and permission-denied states. For this channel: the create form, the edit form (credential field empty, re-entry required), a successful test send and a failed test send with its error code.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Tests ship in the same PR; `make build vet test typecheck` and `cd web && pnpm build` pass; the Postgres suite passes for persistence or migration changes.
- [ ] Docs, `api/openapi.yaml`, `docs/guide/configuration.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` (`Unreleased`) updated where the change touches them (drift guards).
- [ ] New tenant tables have RLS and hostile-harness coverage; new routes have permission tests.
- [ ] No secret, token or credential-bearing URL in logs, errors, attempt rows or API responses.
- [ ] Evidence (section above) is attached to the PR and checked by the reviewer.

## Dependencies

Blocked by: #1367
observacion_a: Implementación de un canal de Telegram; puede involucrar seguridad de integración, pero el contenido principal es funcional.
observacion_b: Vulnerabilidad de impacto moderado o mención genérica.

openDox + openXdox: two open-source layers, an installable app with users, projects and a database; domain descendants pin openXdox (Brett's ruling 2026-09-04)

## Ruling — Brett Heap, 2026-09-04, in session (lane openxfactory-opendox), recorded verbatim

> "we do not have a place to store projects. If i want to start a new project in a new repo, and make some specs, we have no good place to store my projects. I think we need to make this an app that installs and is hosted with a db. we should have users and projects and can expand the feature set."
>
> "openDox is a dead project. it has almost empty repo. I think someone started with idea and stopped after a few days. lets use that name as the core opensource repo. we have two layers of opensource openDox and openXdox. The openXdox is openDox tuned for use with openXfactory. we will make openDox work to just manage documents and ideas. it will keep the integration with git and notebook lm etc and have all tools that help for document management and ideation. then openXdox will integrate with openXfactory."
>
> Earlier in the same sitting: "We then further pin that down to medxDox and CodeXdox for use in those domain factories. If I install MedxFacotry, then I get a medXdox install running in the installed tenand with its own db."

## What the ruling settles

1. **Two open-source layers, two repositories.** `opensoft/openDox` — the neutral core: a hosted, installable app with its own database; users and projects; document and idea management; git and NotebookLM integration and the document-management/ideation tooling. `opensoft/openXdox` — openDox tuned for openxFactory: the corpus reader, doc-health and lifecycle integration, gates, the apply lane. Domain descendants (`MedxDox`, `codexDox`, …) pin openXdox in the `<Domainx><Product>` form; a domain-factory install brings its own descendant instance with its own database in the tenant.
2. **The name `openDox` is taken deliberately.** `docs/openxdox-naming.md` (ratified 2026-08-13) rejected `openDox` as "taken"; Brett has ruled the existing use dead (a near-empty repo abandoned after days) and accepted the name for the core. The record owes an **Amendment 3** carried by the change that creates the repository: it must state the collision facts as measured today — a GitHub organization `opendox` exists, and small repos named `opendox` exist including one active 2026 project in the adjacent agent-written-docs space — and Brett's acceptance of them.
3. **A departure from the wallet precedent, ruled.** `split-openxwallet-repo` kept the integration seam inside openxFactory; here the integration layer is its own open-source repository (`openXdox`). The seam openxFactory keeps is the corpus itself and its governance; what moves to openXdox is the code that reads it.

## Why this is filed as an issue

It is the governing object for the lane's claims (Rule 1) and the place the ruling lives outside a chat transcript. The engineering record it supersedes in part: `openxdox-install-app-provisioning` (staged 2026-08-14, gate met, exit unraised) and codexFactory #89 (standalone migration, open since 2026-08-25) — both fold into the topic this issue commissions.

## What the lane does next

- Brainstorm doc(s) under `ideation/brainstorm/` capturing the two-layer topology, the app-with-database model (users, projects, documents, ideas), the tenant install story, and the openDox/openXdox boundary — the only place contradiction is legal.
- A staging topic under `ideation/staging/` (`opendox-two-layer-product`) with the settled claims from the ruling and the OPEN questions Brett has not yet ruled: what the database is authoritative for versus git; the runtime shape (the Hermes install's FastAPI + Postgres pattern is the in-house precedent); whether a domain install always brings its own instance and database or may point at a shared one; the corpus-adapter boundary that breaks today's two-way `doc_health` ↔ `ideation_dashboard` import cycle; seque

[Feature]: Self-service browser bootstrap/pairing link from an authenticated Control UI (no host CLI required)

## Summary

An already-authenticated operator can self-service pair a **mobile app** from inside Control UI (Devices → **Pair device** → Copy setup code, no terminal needed). There is no equivalent self-service path for pairing a **new browser** (webchat Control UI on a second device/machine). The only documented way to bring up a new browser is `openclaw dashboard` run **on the Gateway host itself** (owner-issued, short-lived, single-use handoff), which requires SSH/console access to that host.

This is a real usability gap for anyone away from the Gateway host who needs to log in from a device that has never been paired before (e.g. a borrowed computer while travelling), and who has no SSH access to the host. Pre-pairing devices in advance is the practical workaround, but there's no self-service recovery path for the "genuinely new browser, no host access" case.

## Why this looks feasible, not just a wish

The mobile "Pair device" setup code and the `openclaw dashboard` browser handoff appear to use the same underlying primitive: a short-lived, single-use signed bootstrap credential (`bootstrapToken=...&bootstrapProfile=owner&gatewayUrl=...` in the `dashboard --json` output). The mobile pairing flow already proves this kind of ephemeral credential can be safely minted from an authenticated `operator.admin` session in the UI, without touching the host. There does not appear to be an architectural reason a "Pair another browser" action couldn't reuse the same mechanism and render it as a copyable link/QR from Devices, gated behind `operator.admin` exactly like mobile pairing is today.

## Related issues

- #141520 — documents the adjacent confusion (pasting a mobile "Pair device" setup code into the Gateway Token field fails with a generic `token_mismatch`). That issue's proposed fix is UI copy/error-message clarity; it does not propose a self-service browser-bootstrap action. Filing this issue separately because it's a capability gap, not a copy/wording bug.
- #120762 / #120764 — improve the *mobile*/LAN/Public-URL pairing wizard's connectivity guidance; scoped to the mobile app flow, not new-browser bootstrap.

## Suggested contract (sketch, not a firm proposal)

1. Devices card gets a second action next to "Pair device": something like **"Pair another browser"**.
2. Gated behind `operator.admin`, same as mobile setup-code creation.
3. Produces a short-lived, single-use link/QR equivalent to what `openclaw dashboard` currently prints from the host CLI (same `bootstrapToken`/`bootstrapProfile=owner` shape), scoped so it can only be redeemed once, by one browser.
4. Documented alongside the existing mobile pairing docs (`/web/control-ui/connect-and-pair#pair-a-mobile-device`) as the browser equivalent.

## Environment where this was noticed

- OpenClaw self-hosted, Docker deployment, token-mode gateway auth.
- Operator already has an admin-paired browser and the OpenClaw mobile app; needed to add a second, previously-unpaired browser while away from the Gateway host.
observacion_a: Flujo de pairing desde una interfaz autenticada; afecta autenticación/autorización y superficie de acceso, aunque es una funcionalidad.

text_content:
fix(ps-service)!: require configured identity for RBAC bootstrap owner grant

## Problem
`resolve_active_roles` (`authz/service.py:176-217`) calls `store.bootstrap_first_owner(principal)` for any principal with no existing rows in `access_role_assignments`. `bootstrap_first_owner` (`authz/store.py:279-327`) grants `SYSTEM_OWNER` to whoever's call wins the advisory lock while the table is empty — reachable from every role-gated MCP tool, with no deliberate "become owner" action and no identity vetting beyond holding a valid token for the configured issuer. In a freshly deployed or re-migrated environment, whichever authenticated user of the same IdP calls first permanently becomes `SystemOwner`.

## Solution
Add operator-configured expected first-owner identity (subject + issuer, matching `Principal.sub`/`Principal.iss`). `bootstrap_first_owner` only grants `SYSTEM_OWNER` when the calling principal matches; a non-matching caller gets no owner grant, the table stays empty, and the response looks identical to an ordinary non-owner call (no disclosure that a bootstrap was attempted or who the real expected owner is). The service fails closed at startup if this identity isn't configured, mirroring the existing OIDC fail-closed pattern (`test_startup_fail_closed`). The advisory lock's existing double-bootstrap protection is preserved unchanged.

## Value
Surfaced by a deep security assessment of the RBAC/ABAC framework (#133). The advisory lock already prevents two simultaneous callers from both becoming owner, but nothing prevents an unintended authenticated user from winning the race to be *first* — meaning permanent, unvetted control over the entire access-role hierarchy could go to whoever reaches the service first, not whoever the deploying organization intended.

## Deliverables
- [ ] New required config for expected first-owner subject + issuer (`ServiceConfig`)
- [ ] `bootstrap_first_owner` compares the calling principal against the configured identity before granting `SYSTEM_OWNER`
- [ ] Startup fails closed with a configuration error when the expected-owner identity is unset
- [ ] Rejected bootstrap attempts recorded as a distinct audit event type

## Discussion
Breaking change: deployments that don't set the new expected-owner config will fail to start. Out of scope: any change to the advisory-locked double-bootstrap protection itself (already correct); any UI/tooling for setting this config beyond the existing env-var config surface.

## Acceptance criteria

### Group 1: Configuration/Startup

| AC-ID | Criterion | Perspective |
|---|---|---|
| AC-BI-001 | WHEN the service starts and the expected first-owner identity (subject + issuer) is not configured THEN the service fails to start with a configuration error, consistent with the existing OIDC fail-closed startup pattern | Security |
| AC-BI-002 | WHEN the expected first-owner identity is configured at startup THEN the service starts normally | Technical |

### Group 2: Authorization/Access

| AC-ID | Criterion | Perspective |
|---|---|---|
| AC-BI-003 | WHEN the `access_role_assignments` table is empty and the calling principal's (sub, iss) matches the configured expected first-owner identity THEN `bootstrap_first_owner` grants that principal `AUTHENTICATED_USER` and `SYSTEM_OWNER` exactly as today | Business |
| AC-BI-004 | WHEN the table is empty and the calling principal's (sub, iss) does NOT match the configured identity THEN `bootstrap_first_owner` does not grant `SYSTEM_OWNER`, the table remains empty, and the caller receives the same response as a normal non-owner call with no indication a bootstrap was attempted or who the expected owner is | Security |

### Group 3: Audit/Logging

| AC-ID | Criterion | Perspective |
|---|---|---|
| AC-BI-005 | WHEN `bootstrap_first_owner` rejects a non-matching principal (AC-BI-004) THEN a distinct audit event is recorded identifying the rejected principal's subject/issuer | Compliance |

## Size
M — single container (ps-serv

DESC: The content parameter appears to be vulnerable to file path manipulation attacks. The payload ../WEB-INF/web.xml was submitted in the content parameter. The file WEB-INF/web.xml was returned.

**Background:**
File path manipulation vulnerabilities arise when user-controllable data is placed into a file or URL path that is used on the server to access local resources, which may be within or outside the web root. If vulnerable, an attacker can modify the file path to access different resources, which may contain sensitive information. Even where an attack is constrained within the web root, it is often possible to retrieve items that are normally protected from direct access, such as application configuration files, the source code for server-executable scripts, or files with extensions that the web server is not configured to serve directly.

**Remediation:**
Ideally, application functionality should be designed in such a way that user-controllable data does not need to be placed into file or URL paths in order to access local resources on the server. This can normally be achieved by referencing known files via an index number rather than their name. If it is considered unavoidable to place user data into file or URL paths, the data should be strictly validated against a whitelist of accepted values. Note that when accessing resources within the web root, simply blocking input containing file path traversal sequences (such as dot-dot-slash) is not always sufficient to prevent retrieval of sensitive information, because some protected items may be accessible at the original path without using any traversal sequences.

fix(gh): turn on `repository-profile.yml` — the repo-topics/description reconciler already built and tested, never installed

Part of the **QwenStorm for vibey 3.0.0**. A sovereign-loop lane (gpt-oss:20b, one instance per model under sub-doctrine 8.c) implements this issue; the result is reviewed and verified before it becomes a pull request. Shared context for every lane: the ratified canon, and the standards this suite enforces (ORM always behind interfaces, comprehensive in-memory fakes so tests need no outside service, the installer installs everything on Arch Linux and macOS).

## Why
`.vibey-gh.toml`'s `[repository_profile]` table already declares this repository's
description and a 15-term topics list (its `enabled` field defaults to `True` —
`src/vibey_tools/gh/vibey_gh/config.py:1034-1055`, `RepositoryProfileConfig`). vibey-gh
already ships a complete, tested GitHub Actions workflow template that reconciles
exactly that data against the live repository —
`src/vibey_tools/gh/vibey_gh/templates/workflows/repository-profile.yml` — which, on
every successful `release-surfaces.yml` run (or manual dispatch), `gh api PATCH
repos/${REPO}` the description and Pages homepage, `gh api PUT repos/${REPO}/topics`
the topics list, sets vulnerability-alert/security-fix flags, reconciles branch
rulesets, and then verifies the live repository actually matches. It is covered by
`src/vibey_tools/gh/test/test_repository_profile.py` and
`src/vibey_tools/gh/test/test_templates.py:2225-2227`. This is precisely "GitHub repo
metadata as code" (sub-doctrine 12.c) — already built, already tested, and simply never
switched on for its own home repository.

The reason it is inert here: `.vibey-gh.toml`'s `[install] workflows` array — the list
`vibey-gh install` actually renders into `.github/workflows/` — is
`["merge-train.yml", "promote-to-main.yml", "provenance.yml", "release-surfaces.yml",
"pr-evaluate.yml", "pr-review.yml", "automation-bootstrap.yml", "github-release.yml",
"conventional-commits.yml"]`. `"repository-profile.yml"` is not in it, and no comment in
the file explains an intentional exclusion. Confirmed: `.github/workflows/` has no
`repository-profile.yml` (`ls .github/workflows/`). The result: the description and 15
topics declared in `.vibey-gh.toml` have reconciled nothing, ever, for this repository —
a search engine and a would-be adopter both see whatever description/topics (if any)
were last set by hand, not the ones this repository actually declares.

## Required behaviour
1. In `.vibey-gh.toml`'s `[install]` table, add `"repository-profile.yml"` to the
   `workflows` array (alongside the nine already listed — order does not matter to
   `vibey-gh install`, but append it last to keep the diff a pure addition).
2. Run `uv run vibey-gh install` (or the equivalent entry point this checkout's
   `vibey-gh` exposes — check `vibey_gh/cli.py`'s `install` subparser if `uv run
   vibey-gh install` is not it) from the repository root. This renders
   `.github/workflows/repository-profile.yml` from the template plus the now-updated
   config. Do not hand-write that file — it must be byte-for-byte what the installer
   renders, or `tools-lint`'s drift check fails it.
3. Commit both `.vibey-gh.toml` and the newly-created `.github/workflows/repository-profile.yml` together.
4. New `tests/meta/test_repository_profile_is_installed.py` asserting:
   - `.vibey-gh.toml`'s parsed `install.workflows` contains `"repository-profile.yml"`.
   - `.github/workflows/repository-profile.yml` exists and its content equals
     `vibey_gh.install.render_workflow(WORKFLOWS / "repository-profile.yml", load_config())`
     called against this repository's own root — i.e. the installed copy is not stale.
     Import `vibey_gh` the same way `src/vibey_tools/gh/test/test_repository_profile.py`
     does (`from vibey_gh import install`, `from vibey_gh.config import load_config`);
     this repository already has `src/vibey_tools/gh` on the path it uses for its own

ZEL Unattended Gate FSM

## Authority
Single unattended controller for ZEL research-to-readiness progression. Immutable GitHub workflow artifacts are SSOT. No stage may advance without an explicit deterministic PASS receipt.

## Global locks
- Maximum one heavy VPS replay at a time.
- No duplicate strategy+axis+data-SHA replay.
- No canonical, registry, runtime, Formal Ledger, Shadow, Paper, Live, or order mutation during research stages.
- `selection_authority=false`, `promotion_authority=false`, `execution_authority=NONE`, `order_authority=BLOCKED` until the applicable later gate explicitly passes.
- Live/order remains forbidden without explicit user approval.

## Ordered stages
- [x] G0 Accept PR #559 exit-contract artifact
- [x] G1 Merge staged PR #564 into PR #560 head; accept EMA artifact
- [x] G2 Merge staged PR #565 into PR #562 head; accept Scalp artifact
- [x] G3 Finalize all 25 strategy dispositions
- [ ] G4 Produce 2–3 economic survivors or exhaust approved repair axes
- [ ] G5 Independent OOS/walk-forward/stress validation

Every candidate must have exact source-owner and baseline trade/economic-digest parity; W1-only selection frozen through W2/W3; complete fee/slippage/funding lineage; errors=0; duplicate=0; censored-open=0; unknown-exit=0 where applicable; no future MFE/MAE leakage; no protected mutation. Economic survivor requires W1, W2, and W3 each: Net R>0, PF>=1, expectancy>0, payoff>=1, retention>=60%.

## Failure handling
Implementation/infrastructure defects: read-only diagnosis → one root cause → minimum patch → verify → at most two retries. Economic failure is recorded as terminal evidence and moves only to the next distinct approved causal axis; it is never treated as PASS. Secret/permission/quota/external-service blockers or the same cause failing twice force HOLD and user-authority request.

## User inspection
The controller must maintain one latest-state comment on this issue containing: stage, active PR/run/job, head SHA, artifact SHA, PASS/FAIL/HOLD, gate evidence, retry count, current blocker, next permitted action, and confirmation that Live/order authority is blocked. [P2][Téléchargements][Notifications] Alerter quand Sonarr ou Radarr ne trouve aucune release

## Besoin produit — 19 septembre 2026

Lorsqu’un téléchargement est lancé puis que **Sonarr ou Radarr ne trouve aucune release compatible**, l’utilisateur peut quitter l’écran sans savoir que la demande a échoué.

Attendu : recevoir une **notification utilisateur explicite** lorsque la recherche aboutit réellement à « aucun résultat ».

Baseline canonique : `main` `93639c29e19ea629fa3e3c4dc4fd15ae86267c6a`.

## État actuel

- Le lifecycle SeenIt sait passer une demande en `error` et afficher un toast local.
- Le fallback épisode sait déjà distinguer « aucune release isolée / aucun pack compatible ».
- Les notifications système de fin de téléchargement sont actuellement émises via **webhooks Sonarr/Radarr -> FCM**.
- Aucun contrat dédié retrouvé pour notifier l’échec « aucune release trouvée ».

Un toast local ne suffit pas si l’utilisateur a quitté l’app ou lancé le téléchargement depuis un autre support.

## Contrat cible

Quand une demande explicite SeenIt arrive à une conclusion fiable « aucune release compatible trouvée » :
- l’état du téléchargement passe en erreur avec message lisible ;
- l’utilisateur reçoit une notification liée au même UID ;
- la notification nomme le média SeenIt et, pour une série, le scope saison/épisode ;
- elle ne montre pas de nom brut de torrent ou détail technique inutile ;
- elle n’est envoyée qu’une fois par demande / résultat d’échec ;
- un timeout, une panne réseau ou un service indisponible ne doivent pas être présentés comme « aucun résultat » ;
- si un fallback pack est encore en cours, ne pas notifier trop tôt.

## Architecture attendue

Réutiliser l’infrastructure de notifications liée au compte/appareils existante plutôt que créer un canal parallèle fragile.

Le déclencheur exact doit être placé là où l’absence de résultat est **définitive et prouvée** pour la demande, avec clé d’idempotence `requestId`.

## Critères d’acceptation

- [ ] Radarr : zéro release admissible -> état erreur + notification.
- [ ] Sonarr épisode/saison/série : zéro release admissible après tous les fallbacks autorisés -> état erreur + notification.
- [ ] Panne/timeout/auth KO -> message de panne distinct, jamais « aucun résultat ».
- [ ] Aucun doublon de notification lors des polls/retries.
- [ ] Notification rattachée au bon UID et aux appareils autorisés.
- [ ] Titre média issu de l’intention SeenIt canonique, jamais du torrent brut.
- [ ] Tap notification ouvre SeenIt sur un contexte utile si l’infrastructure existante le permet.
- [ ] TNR succès / aucun résultat / panne / retry / idempotence.
- [ ] Parité demande lancée depuis APK ou PWA.

Priorité : **P2** — feedback asynchrone indispensable pour une action potentiellement longue.

[VULN ALERT] CVE-2026-75971 (risk 42.0) - wordpress/wordpress

**CVE:** CVE-2026-75971
**Composite risk score:** 42.0/100 (35% CVSS + 40% EPSS + 25% KEV bonus -- see dashboard footer for methodology)
**Source:** nvd
**CVSS score:** 7.2 (CVSS V31)
**EPSS score:** unknown
**In CISA KEV:** No
**Affected vendor/product:** wordpress/wordpress
**Matched keywords:** wordpress
**Published:** 2026-08-25T12:16:25.087

**Description:**
The ShopEngine Elementor WooCommerce Builder Addon – All in One WooCommerce Solution plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 4.9.4. This is due to the `rum_importer()` function being registered on the WordPress core `import_start` action hook with no plugin-owned capability check and no allowlist filtering, causing arbitrary `<wp_option>` name/value pairs parsed from an attacker-supplied WXR import file to be passed directly to `update_option()`. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Shop Manager-level access and above, to write arbitrary WordPress options — most critically setting `users_can_register` to `1` and `default_role` to `administrator` — enabling open self-registration of Administrator accounts and full site takeover. This is exploitable by Shop Manager-level users because WooCommerce grants that role the `import` capability, allowing it to reach the WordPress Importer flow that fires the `import_start` hook on which `rum_importer()` is registered, contrary to the assumption that the hook is restricted to Administrators.

- [ ] Check for available patch / upgrade path

[P2] Preserve parent template flows rendered through block.super

When a child overrides a Django template block and renders `{{ block.super }}`, filter applications in the parent block are removed from render-context flow analysis even though Django executes them.

Observed on engine 0.18.0, commit `5610778`.

### Reproduction

```django
{# app/templates/app/base.html #}
{% block body %}{{ bio|striptags }}{% endblock %}
```

```django
{# app/templates/app/profile.html #}
{% extends 'app/base.html' %}
{% block body %}{{ block.super }}{% endblock %}
```

Render `app/profile.html` with `{'bio': request.POST['bio']}` as the context, using the vulnerable Django/advisory setup for the `striptags` entry point.

Actual result: the filter remains reachable, but the exploitable context-to-filter flow disappears. A child that leaves the parent's block intact preserves that flow.

### Location and ownership

- [Replaced blocks are excluded](https://github.com/CoreTrace/coretrace-python-analyzer/blob/5610778/src/coretrace_python/taint/templates.py#L374-L380)
- [The overridden set is propagated to the parent](https://github.com/CoreTrace/coretrace-python-analyzer/blob/5610778/src/coretrace_python/taint/templates.py#L439-L453)

Model `block.super` in template inheritance/context-flow composition so parent applications are retained when the child renders them. Do not retain every overridden parent block unconditionally: a complete replacement must still exclude the parent flow.

### Acceptance criteria

- The reproduction retains the flow from `bio` to the parent's `striptags` application, with the parent template location as evidence.
- A replacement block without `block.super` still excludes that parent flow.
- Unrelated overridden blocks do not become reachable through another block's `super`.
- Nested inheritance preserves the appropriate parent chain without duplicate findings.
observacion_a: Problema de renderizado de templates en Django sin evidencia de impacto de seguridad en el texto.
observacion_b: Vulnerabilidad de impacto moderado o mención genérica.

Governance: RCS protocol master (tightened, all unique rules)

# RCS protocol master (tightened, all unique rules)

Planning record only. No Version B, consent UI, biometric collection, Railway, or production merge from this issue.

Related: #219, #280, #282.

Default protocol governs feature scope, lawful purpose, data categories, agreement version, visible notice, applicable consent, minimum-necessary use, access controls, retention, audit logging, review, and release approval.

---

## Agreement

A signed site-entry agreement records version, timestamp, user identity or account identifier, and optional feature categories the user affirmatively selected.

A general site-entry agreement applies only to selected features and stated purposes. It does not expand a feature beyond its stated purpose or authorize undisclosed analysis of sensitive signals.

The platform may process information only inside those categories, purposes, and data uses.

## Analysis under the default protocol

Categories: user-provided planning information; user-selected accessibility settings; stated communication format; stated goals, constraints, and time horizon; meeting content only when the participant has notice and applicable recording or analysis terms are satisfied.

Permitted pattern analysis: identify stated questions; organize stated topics; identify missing documents or facts; map stated assumptions to scenario inputs; identify source categories relevant to those questions; generate a neutral question list; identify contradictions in participant-provided facts for clarification; suggest a pause, clarification, second opinion, or no-action path.

Objective analysis uses participant-provided information, disclosed meeting content, selected preferences, and source-supported planning inputs. It presents questions, assumptions, risks, limitations, alternatives, sources, and professional-review needs in clear form.

Decision-support: help the participant understand documented options and prepare questions for qualified professionals.

Decision-control: the participant retains every financial, legal, tax, insurance, lending, estate, and investment decision.

## Sensitive-inference list (one list, two uses)

Signals: heart rate; heart-rate variability; facial expression; eye movement; pupil size; voice stress; breathing rate; webcam data; wearable data; typing behavior; mouse behavior; browsing behavior; email behavior; transcript sentiment; inferred excitement, anxiety, confidence, vulnerability, mental-health condition, or financial susceptibility; body language.

Hard bans (always): targeting; pricing; eligibility; suitability; product ranking; referral ranking; lead routing or scoring; behavioral manipulation; hidden persuasion; covert steering; personalized urgency, scarcity, fear, or shame; financial-decision prediction or steering; predicting or optimizing probability of yes, next-step, product selection, referral, financing, investment, estate-plan change, or a transaction.

Research hold: any future use of this list requires a separate scoped issue, legal and privacy review, security design, user controls, purpose limitation, retention limits, non-discrimination review, and release approval.

Audio, visual, or interaction features cannot collect or infer these traits without the default protocol and an approved lawful purpose.

If a feature ever uses any item on this list, it must be visible, optional where applicable, explained in plain language, user-controllable, removable under the default protocol, and limited to accessibility, comprehension, meeting organization, or user-selected presentation. Hidden biometric inference to influence a financial decision is forbidden.

## Meeting analysis

Before recording, transcription, language-pattern analysis, body-signal analysis, state-transition modeling, or AI-assisted modeling: give notice of the activity, purpose, data categories, retention, access, systems, and consent choice. Operate only
observacion_a: Define controles de propósito, acceso, retención, auditoría y consentimiento; es gobernanza de seguridad/privacidad.

Project Charter: Detección de intrusiones en redes con ML

# Project Charter: Detección de intrusiones en redes con Machine Learning

Inteligencia Artificial - Ingeniería en Informática - UNDEF CRUC IUA

- **Docente:** Ing. Hernando Alexis González
- **Modalidad:** Grupal
- **Integrantes:** Maximo Agustin Rodeyro y Lautaro Niccolini
- **Categorías:** Machine Learning Predictivo y Data Engineering & IA
- **Fecha:** 28/9/2026

## 1. Resumen

La idea del proyecto es armar un sistema de detección de intrusiones (NIDS) basado en Machine Learning. El sistema recibe los datos de un flujo de red (protocolo, servicio, duración, bytes y paquetes enviados en cada sentido, TTL, etc.) y decide si ese flujo es tráfico normal o un ataque. Como segunda tarea, también intentamos predecir de qué tipo de ataque se trata.

Para esto usamos el dataset UNSW-NB15 con la división en train y test que publicaron sus autores. Vamos a comparar una regla simple sin IA y una regresión logística contra XGBoost, validar con cross-validation sobre el train y evaluar el modelo final una sola vez sobre el test. Al final queremos tener un pipeline reproducible y un script de consola que reciba un CSV con flujos y devuelva las predicciones.

## 2. Definición del problema

Los IDS tradicionales funcionan con firmas, es decir, reglas escritas a mano para ataques ya conocidos, y les cuesta detectar variantes nuevas. Nuestra propuesta es entrenar un modelo que aprenda cómo se comporta el tráfico malicioso a partir de ejemplos etiquetados, para que funcione como una capa más de detección.

Planteamos dos tareas sobre los mismos datos:

- **Binaria (tarea principal):** normal o ataque.
- **Multiclase (tarea secundaria):** Normal o una de las 9 categorías de ataque del dataset (Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, Exploits, Fuzzers, Generic, Reconnaissance, Shellcode y Worms).

### PEAS

| | |
|---|---|
| Performance | Tarea binaria: recall de ataques y tasa de falsos positivos, además de F1 y PR-AUC. Tarea multiclase: Macro-F1 y F1 por clase. |
| Environment | Registros de flujos de red del dataset UNSW-NB15. Es un entorno parcialmente observable porque solo tenemos los metadatos del flujo y no el contenido de los paquetes. Es estático, ya que trabajamos sobre archivos CSV. |
| Actuators | Para cada flujo, el sistema devuelve una etiqueta (normal/ataque o categoría de ataque) junto con su probabilidad. |
| Sensors | Las 42 variables que trae cada registro: protocolo, servicio, estado de la conexión, duración, bytes y paquetes por sentido, TTL, pérdidas, jitter, tiempos del handshake TCP, tamaño medio de los paquetes y contadores de conexiones recientes. |

## 3. Datos

Usamos UNSW-NB15, un dataset armado por el Australian Centre for Cyber Security de UNSW Canberra (Moustafa y Slay, 2015). Lo descargamos desde la página oficial (research.unsw.edu.au/projects/unsw-nb15-dataset). Trabajamos solamente con la partición en train y test que publicaron los autores:

- `UNSW_NB15_training-set.csv`: 175.341 registros.
- `UNSW_NB15_testing-set.csv`: 82.332 registros.

Cada registro tiene 45 columnas. De esas, 42 son las variables que usamos como entrada (39 numéricas y 3 categóricas: `proto`, `service` y `state`). Las otras tres son `id`, que es un índice de fila y se descarta, y las dos etiquetas: `label` (0 = normal, 1 = ataque) y `attack_cat` (la categoría del ataque, o "Normal").

También existe una copia del dataset en Kaggle, pero ahí los archivos de train y test tienen los nombres cambiados. Por eso usamos la versión oficial y verificamos los archivos con su hash MD5 antes de entrenar. Los hashes y los pasos para descargar los datos están en `data/README.md`.

Cuando revisamos los datos encontramos varias cosas a tener en cuenta:

- **No hay valores faltantes.** Algunos valores de `state` aparecen solo en el test, así que el encoding de las variables categóricas tiene que soportar categorías que no vio en el entrenamiento.
- **Desbalance.** En el train el 68 % de los registros son ata
observacion_a: Proyecto de detección de intrusiones de red mediante ML; seguridad es el objetivo central.
observacion_b: Vulnerabilidad de impacto moderado o mención genérica.

It validates those same public values and has no external configuration override. [`Program.cs`](https://github.com/realworld-apps/aspnetcore-realworld-example-app/blob/a397d1197b22edeffa4d2563fa5f4f7f11d0b254/src/Conduit/Program.cs#L99-L112) registers `AddJwt()` and calls `UseAuthentication()`. [`ProfilesController`](https://github.com/realworld-apps/aspnetcore-realworld-example-app/blob/a397d1197b22edeffa4d2563fa5f4f7f11d0b254/src/Conduit/Features/Profiles/ProfilesController.cs#L8-L13) exposes profile lookups without authorization. [`UserController`](https://github.com/realworld-apps/aspnetcore-realworld-example-app/blob/a397d1197b22edeffa4d2563fa5f4f7f11d0b254/src/Conduit/Features/Users/UserController.cs#L11-L26) protects the current-user endpoints with JWT authentication. [`CurrentUserAccessor`](https://github.com/realworld-apps/aspnetcore-realworld-example-app/blob/a397d1197b22edeffa4d2563fa5f4f7f11d0b254/src/Conduit/Infrastructure/CurrentUserAccessor.cs#L7-L12) treats the token’s subject as the current username. [`Edit.Handler`](https://github.com/realworld-apps/aspnetcore-realworld-example-app/blob/a397d1197b22edeffa4d2563fa5f4f7f11d0b254/src/Conduit/Features/Users/Edit.cs#L119-L194) loads that account, accepts a new password, saves its new hash, and returns a token for it. ## Proof of concept Use an existing username on an instance running the default code. CI flake : le skip storm vient d'un crash DLL de torch (0xc0000138), pas de la JVM

## Ce qui est mesuré

Le « skip storm » qui fait rougir des jobs `automated-tests` par intermittence **n'est pas** un problème de JVM ni de JPype. La cause première est un échec de chargement de DLL natif de **torch** :

```
Windows fatal exception: code 0xc0000138

Thread 0x00000e84 (most recent call first):
  File "C:\Miniconda\envs\projet-is\lib\site-packages\torch\__init__.py", line 125 in <module>
  ...
  File "..._pytest\python.py", line 508 in importtestmodule
  File "..._pytest\main.py", line 394 in pytest_collection
```

`0xc0000138` = `STATUS_ORDINAL_NOT_FOUND` : une DLL est trouvée mais n'exporte pas l'ordinal attendu par un dépendant. C'est un conflit de chargement natif, pas une erreur Python — d'où l'absence de traceback exploitable jusqu'ici.

La suite est mécanique et **le garde fait son travail** : la JVM finit non démarrée, la fixture `jvm_session` (`tests/conftest.py:513`) saute chaque test, et le garde #1385 dans `ci.yml` refuse le badge vert d'un run qui n'a rien décidé. **Le garde n'est pas le bug** — il est ce qui a rendu le défaut visible.

## Preuve que ce n'est pas le contenu d'une branche

Comparaison équilibrée, les deux côtés sur la **même** branche :

| run | commit | résultat |
|---|---|---|
| `31131562078` | `main` @ `d6415011` | **rouge** — 3× `0xc0000138`, 13839 skipped, 0 passed |
| `31132969667` | `main` @ `8775e167` (commit suivant) | **vert** — 13578 passed |

Et sur PR, à ~7 min d'écart le même soir :

| run | PR | résultat |
|---|---|---|
| `31133365400` | #1642 | 13578 passed (2 échecs de contenu, réels) |
| `31130615589` (att. 3) | #1639 | 13841 skipped, 0 passed |

## Ce qui est écarté par la mesure

Les deux côtés installent **la même chose** — vérifié dans les logs des quatre runs :

- `pytorch 2.2.2`, `numpy 1.25.0` (conda, même solve)
- `JPype1 1.7.1` (pip)
- `JAVA_HOME` = Temurin `11.0.31-11`

Donc ni la version de torch, ni celle de numpy, ni celle de JPype, ni celle du JDK ne discriminent. Une campagne antérieure avait déjà écarté la version du JDK sur un 2×2 (`11.0.31-11` et `11.0.32-9`, chacune des deux côtés). **La variable causale n'a pas encore été trouvée** — et c'est précisément ce que cette issue demande de chercher, pas de supposer.

## Piste à instruire (hypothèse, pas conclusion)

`STATUS_ORDINAL_NOT_FOUND` au chargement de torch évoque une DLL de l'image runner (runtime MSVC, `libiomp5md.dll`, MKL, ou une DLL apportée par un outil préinstallé) qui se trouve devant celle attendue dans l'ordre de recherche. Ce qui varie d'un run à l'autre serait alors le **PATH effectif de l'image**, pas le contenu de l'environnement conda. À vérifier, pas à croire :

1. Logger `os.environ["PATH"]` et le résultat de `os.add_dll_directory` au tout début de la session pytest, et **comparer un run rouge à un run vert**. Sans cette comparaison on n'aura qu'une hypothèse de plus.
2. Capturer le nom de la DLL fautive (`dumpbin /dependents`, ou `torch`'s `_load_dll_libraries` en mode verbeux) — l'ordinal manquant nomme le coupable.
3. Compter la fréquence réelle sur les 30 derniers runs de `main` avant de dimensionner un remède. Un flake à 5 % et un flake à 40 % n'appellent pas la même réponse.

## Ce qu'il ne faut PAS faire

- **Ne pas** neutraliser le garde #1385. Il transforme un run qui ne décide rien en échec — c'est exactement ce qu'on veut. Le désarmer rendrait le défaut invisible sans le corriger.
- **Ne pas** ajouter un `try/except` autour de l'import de torch. Cela remplacerait un crash bruyant par une session muette où les tests torch passeraient en skip sans que personne ne le sache — le motif exact que le garde existe pour empêcher.
- **Ne pas** conclure sur une version. Quatre runs, deux verts deux rouges, versions identiques partout : la conclusion « c'est torch 2.2.2 » est déjà réfutée.
- **Ne pas** relancer indéfiniment. Un rerun est légitime quand le job n'a testé **aucune** ligne de la PR ;

### Bounty Proposal: $50 USDC

**Target:** `backend/routers/oauth.py`
**Pull Request:** https://github.com/BasedHardware/omi/pull/19715

- Validated with hermetic unit tests in `backend/tests/unit/test_oauth_token_async_boundaries.py` (5/5 tests pass).

CVE: 2026-53550 found in js-yaml - Version: 3.14.1 [JS]

Veracode Software Composition Analysis  
===============================
  
 Attribute | Details  
| --- | --- |  
Library | js-yaml  
Description | YAML 1.2 parser and serializer  
Language | JS  
Vulnerability | JS-YAML: Quadratic-complexity DoS In Merge Key Handling Via Repeated Aliases  
Vulnerability description | Summary
A crafted YAML document can trigger algorithmic CPU exhaustion in "js-yaml" merge-key processing ("<<") by repeating the same alias many times in a merge sequence.
This causes quadratic parse-time behavior relative to input size and can block a Node.js worker/event loop for seconds with a relatively small payload (tens of KB), resulting in denial of service.
Details
The issue is in merge handling inside "lib/loader.js":
- "storeMappingPair(...)" iterates every element of a merge sequence when key tag is "tag:yaml.org,2002:merge".
- For each element, it calls "mergeMappings(...)".
- "mergeMappings(...)" computes "Object.keys(source)" and performs "_hasOwnProperty.call(destination, key)" checks for each key.
When input is of the form:
a: &a {k0:0, k1:0, ..., kK:0}
b: {<<: [*a, *a, *a, ... repeated M times ...]}
all *a entries refer to the same anchored object. After the first merge, subsequent merges are semantically no-ops, but the parser still reprocesses all keys each time.
Resulting work is O(K * M), while input size is O(K + M), giving quadratic scaling as payload grows.
Relevant code path:
lib/loader.js in storeMappingPair(...) merge branch (keyTag === 'tag:yaml.org,2002:merge')
lib/loader.js mergeMappings(...)
Root cause
File:       lib/loader.js
Function:   storeMappingPair(state, _result, overridableKeys, keyTag, keyNode,
valueNode, startLine, startLineStart, startPos)
Lines:      ~359-366
if (keyTag === 'tag:yaml.org,2002:merge') {
  if (Array.isArray(valueNode)) {
    for (index = 0, quantity = valueNode.length; index < quantity; index += 1) {
      mergeMappings(state, _result, valueNode[index], overridableKeys);
    }
  } else {
    mergeMappings(state, _result, valueNode, overridableKeys);
  }
}
When the merge value is a sequence (YAML 1.1 <<: [ *a, *a, ... ]), each element
is handed to mergeMappings() without deduplication. mergeMappings() then does
sourceKeys = Object.keys(source);
for (index = 0; index < sourceKeys.length; index += 1) {
  key = sourceKeys[index];
  if (!_hasOwnProperty.call(destination, key)) {
    setProperty(destination, key, source[key]);
    overridableKeys[key] = true;
  }
}
Every alias reference in the sequence resolves (by design) to the SAME object
via state.anchorMap. After the first merge, every subsequent merge of that same
reference is a pure no-op semantically, but still performs:
* one Object.keys(source) call (O(K))
* K _hasOwnProperty.call checks on the destination
Total: M * K hasOwnProperty checks + M Object.keys allocations, while the final
object and all observable side effects are identical to a single merge.
YAML semantics for "<<:" are idempotent and commutative over duplicate sources,
so collapsing duplicates preserves behavior exactly; this isn't a spec trade-off.
PoC
Environment:
js-yaml version: 4.1.1
Node.js: v24.5.0
Platform: arm64 macOS (reproduced consistently)
Reproduction script:
Create many keys in one anchored map (&a).
Merge that same alias repeatedly via <<: [*a, *a, ...].
Measure parse time and compare with control payload using single merge (<<: *a).
Observed repeated runs (same machine):
K=M=1000, input 9,909 bytes: ~33–36 ms
K=M=2000, input 20,909 bytes: ~121–123 ms
K=M=4000, input 42,909 bytes: ~524–537 ms
K=M=6000, input 64,909 bytes: ~1,608–1,829 ms
K=M=8000, input 86,909 bytes: ~3,395–3,565 ms
Control (single merge, similar key counts):
K=2000: ~1–2 ms
K=4000: ~3 ms
K=8000: ~5 ms
Also verified: repeated-merge output equals single-merge output (same key count and same JSON), confirming excess time

Plex token forwarded to third-party hosts on cross-origin redirects

## Summary

`PlexClient.request()` in `packages/plex/src/client.ts` issues `fetch` with the default redirect mode (`follow`) and attaches the `X-Plex-Token` header on every request. When the configured Plex server answers with a redirect to a different origin, the fetch is followed automatically and the `X-Plex-Token` header is forwarded to the redirect target, disclosing the Plex token to a third-party host.

## Severity

Medium (security - credential disclosure). A Plex token grants full access to the user's Plex account on that server. Exploitation requires control of, or a MITM position on, the configured server endpoint - made easier by the fact that `normalisePlexBaseUrl` accepts plain `http://` addresses. Same-origin redirect loops are also silently followed.

## Reproduction

Verified against main (0312d88) with two loopback fixtures:

```js
// Server A (the "Plex server"): 302 -> Server B
// Server B records inbound headers
const client = new PlexClient(`http://127.0.0.1:${portA}`, 'SECRET-TOKEN')
await client.testConnection()
// Server B received: X-Plex-Token: SECRET-TOKEN
```

Observed: the redirect is followed and the second host receives the full `X-Plex-Token` value. (The redirect spans origins - different port - and the token still arrives.)

## Affected code

- `PlexClient.request()` (~line 345): `fetch(`${this.baseUrl}${path}`, { ... })` with no `redirect` option.
- `plexTvRequest()` has the same shape, though its origin is pinned to `https://plex.tv` so exposure is lower.

## Expected

text_content:
Plugin loader: BasePluginRegistry, manifest validation, lifecycle, DI isolation

## Context

Generalize the existing gateway pattern (`GatewayRegistryService`, gateway lifecycle, config-update pub/sub, disable-on-failure) into a category-aware plugin host. Existing data gateways become `category: DataGateway` plugins via the port/registry retrofit in #193; **no DataGateway ships bundled** (#194) — BGG/IGDB are official registry-published plugins. New categories (notification, storage, media integration) plug into the same lifecycle.

> **Amended 2026-07 under epic #192**: scoped grant model (`PluginGrant`), consent-unit update semantics, `executionMode` (#197), `topics` (#196), DataGateway de-bundling (#194). Scheduling/pre-consent for updates lives in #199.

**Authorization model:** Plugins are *installed principals*, not delegations of user authority. Once installed and granted permissions, the plugin operates with its own authority. There is no runtime intersection with a "triggering user" — the trigger field on the plugin actor is for audit attribution only. See #68 (AbilityService) for the resolution surface.

**Grants are scoped and manifest-versioned.** Authority is layered by consent unit:

- Server-scope grants: made by the server admin at install/update
- Household/user-scope grants: made by the household admin / user when enabling or configuring the plugin for their scope

The plugin actor's ability resolution intersects with the grants of the consent unit it is operating in (household/user context from CLS). One active code version per server; grant sets may differ per unit.

**Distribution model:** Tarball-based with mandatory SHA-256 verification. URL fetch or manual upload. No npm-registry install at the server (supply-chain attack surface). See #84 for full distribution spec, registry manifest, and release channels.

## Scope

### Data model

```
Plugin {
  id            String   @id
  slug          String   @unique
  version       String
  category      PluginCategory
  scope         PluginScope    // Server | Household
  manifestJson  Json
  bundled       Boolean        // no DataGateway rows are bundled (#194); applies to e.g. local-disk storage driver
  enabled       Boolean
  loadFailed    Boolean
  loadError     String?
  installedAt   DateTime
  installedById String
  updatedAt     DateTime

  // Distribution provenance (#84):
  installedFromUrl      String?
  installedSha256       String
  registrySlug          String?

  // Permission-escalating update flow (scheduling extensions in #199):
  pendingVersion       String?
  pendingManifestJson  Json?
  pendingSince         DateTime?

  // Update check (#84):
  updateCheckEnabled   Boolean   @default(false)
  updateCheckUrl       String?
  lastUpdateCheckAt    DateTime?
  latestKnownVersion   String?
}

HouseholdPlugin {
  id            String   @id
  householdId   String
  pluginId      String
  enabled       Boolean
  config        Json
  enabledById   String
  enabledAt     DateTime

  @@unique([householdId, pluginId])
}

PluginGrant {
  id              String   @id
  pluginId        String
  scopeType       PluginGrantScope   // Server | Household | User
  scopeId         String?            // null for Server
  permissionSlug  String
  manifestVersion String             // the manifest version this consent was given against
  grantedById     String
  grantedAt       DateTime
  effectiveFrom   DateTime?          // pre-consent dormancy, see #199

  @@unique([pluginId, scopeType, scopeId, permissionSlug])
}
```

### Manifest type & JSON schema

```ts
type LocalizedString = string | Record<string, string>;

interface PluginFeatureDeclaration {
  name: string;
  displayName: LocalizedString;
  description: LocalizedString;
}

interface PluginPermissionRequest {
  slug: string;
  required: boolean;
  reason: LocalizedString;
  feature?: string;
  consentScope?: 'server' | 'household' | 'user';   // default 'server'; who must consent to grant it
}

**Background:**
Reflected cross-site scripting vulnerabilities arise when data is copied from a request and echoed into the application's immediate response in an unsafe way. An attacker can use the vulnerability to construct a request that, if issued by another application user, will cause JavaScript code supplied by the attacker to execute within the user's browser in the context of that user's session with the application. The attacker-supplied code can perform a wide variety of actions, such as stealing the victim's session token or login credentials, performing arbitrary actions on the victim's behalf, and logging their keystrokes. Users can be induced to issue the attacker's crafted request in various ways. For example, the attacker can send a victim a link containing a malicious URL in an email or instant message. They can submit the link to popular web sites that allow content authoring, for example in blog comments. And they can create an innocuous looking web site that causes anyone viewing it to make arbitrary cross-domain requests to the vulnerable application (using either the GET or the POST method). The security impact of cross-site scripting vulnerabilities is dependent upon the nature of the vulnerable application, the kinds of data and functionality that it contains, and the other applications that belong to the same domain and organization. If the application is used only to display non-sensitive public content, with no authentication or access control functionality, then a cross-site scripting flaw may be considered low risk. However, if the same application resides on a domain that can access cookies for other more security-critical applications, then the vulnerability could be used to attack those other applications, and so may be considered high risk. Similarly, if the organization that owns the application is a likely target for phishing attacks, then the vulnerability could be leveraged to lend credibility to such attacks, by injecting Trojan functionality into the vulnerable application and exploiting users' trust in the organization in order to capture credentials for other applications that it owns. In many kinds of application, such as those providing online banking functionality, cross-site scripting should always be considered high risk.

**Remediation:**
In most situations where user-controllable data is copied into application responses, cross-site scripting attacks can be prevented using two layers of defenses: Input should be validated as strictly as possible on arrival, given the kind of content that it is expected to contain. Windows bounded mode: platform adapter attests no identity for desktop processes, making every application grant unmatchable

### Primary area

Cua Driver

### Summary

On Windows, `list_apps` reports running desktop-kind processes with `bundle_id`, `launch_path` and `executable` all null, so `resource_matches_application()` has nothing to compare a capability manifest entry against and can never match. Bounded mode consequently refuses every action on every application — it behaves as deny-everything rather than deny-by-default, leaving `--permission-mode standard` (no resource scoping at all) as the only usable configuration on Windows.

### Reproduction

1. Install cua-driver 0.21.0 on Windows 10/11.

2. Create a v3 capability manifest granting a single app. Note `bundle_id` and `executable` are mutually exclusive — declaring both fails validation at startup with `each application resource must declare exactly one of bundle_id or executable`:

```yaml
version: 3
expires_after: 8h
idle_timeout: 30m

allow:
  tools:
    - start_session
    - end_session
    - launch_app
    - list_windows
    - list_apps
    - get_window_state
    - get_accessibility_tree
    - click
    - type_text
    - drag

resources:
  apps:
    - bundle_id: 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe'
      launch: true
      windows: all
  desktop:
    display: true
```

3. Start a bounded daemon:

```
cua-driver serve --permission-mode bounded --capability-manifest <path> --approve-capability-manifest
```

4. With Chrome running, call `list_apps`. It succeeds — but the Chrome record has null identity fields (see Evidence).

5. Call `list_windows`. It succeeds and returns Chrome's windows with pid and window_id.

6. Call `get_window_state` or `capture` against that pid and window_id.

Reproduces 100% of the time, for every application, with every manifest spelling tried: `bundle_id` alone, `executable` alone, both together, forward slashes and backslashes.

### Expected behavior

An application declared in the capability manifest should match the corresponding running process, so that `get_window_state`, `capture` and input calls against that application's windows succeed, while applications absent from the manifest are refused with `bounded_resource_outside_manifest`.

That is, bounded mode should be deny-by-default with a working allowlist.

### Actual behavior

Every application is refused, including the one declared in the manifest:

```
protected resource is outside the capability manifest: desktop pid 15092 window 66850 is outside the capability manifest
```

The cause is visible in `list_apps`: running desktop-kind processes carry no identity fields at all. `resource_matches_application()` matches on `bundle_id`, `fingerprint.executable`, `executable` or `launch_path`:

```rust
let bundle_id = resource.get("bundle_id").and_then(serde_json::Value::as_str);
let executable = resource
    .pointer("/fingerprint/executable")
    .or_else(|| resource.get("executable"))
    .or_else(|| resource.get("launch_path"))
    .and_then(serde_json::Value::as_str);
```

For Windows desktop-kind resources the adapter supplies none of these, so both resolve to `None`, `is_some_and(...)` is false for every grant, and the match fails unconditionally.

Note `bundle_id` is a macOS concept. On Windows the adapter does populate it for *registered/installed* apps (AppX package family names such as `Microsoft.WindowsCalculator_8wekyb3d8bbwe`, and Start-menu paths such as `...\Application\chrome_proxy.exe`), but not for the running desktop processes that windows actually belong to. A manifest can therefore only address entries that cannot be acted upon.

I have not verified whether the root cause is the adapter omitting the fields, or redaction applied to unmatched resources before comparison — see Evidence for why I suspect the latter.

### Environment

- Cua component and version: cua-driver 0.21.0 (Windows), installed at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Cua\cua

SEC-005: Thread-Local Buffer Reuse Makes C++ API Unsafe


| Severity | **Low** |
| File | `ffi/zvec_ffi.cc:1140-1560` |
| Impact | Data corruption if C++ API consumers do not copy results immediately (PHP FFI layer is safe) |
| CVSS | 4.4 (AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L) |
| Status | Open |

## Problem

Multiple getter functions in `zvec_ffi.cc` use `thread_local` static buffers to return data. Each call overwrites the previous buffer content. The PHP FFI layer is protected because `FFI::string()` copies data immediately from C pointers to PHP strings, but:

1. Any future C++ consumer of this API must be aware that returned pointers are only valid until the next call to the same function
2. The sparse vector getters use a circular buffer of only 16 slots — calling `getSparseVector*` on more than 16 fields overwrites earlier results
3. The single-slot buffers (`g_pk_buf`, `g_string_buf`, `g_vector_buf`, etc.) make the C++ API inherently unsafe for direct use

## Affected Code

```cpp
// ffi/zvec_ffi.cc:1140-1145
static thread_local std::string g_pk_buf;
const char* zvec_doc_get_pk(zvec_doc_t doc) {
    g_pk_buf = static_cast<Doc*>(doc)->pk();
    return g_pk_buf.c_str();  // pointer invalidated on next call
}

// ffi/zvec_ffi.cc:1260-1278 — sparse vector circular buffer (16 slots)
static thread_local std::array<
    std::pair<std::vector<uint32_t>, std::vector<float>>, 16
> g_sparse_buffers;
static thread_local size_t g_sparse_buffer_idx = 0;

int zvec_doc_get_sparse_vector_fp32(zvec_doc_t doc, const char* field,
    const uint32_t** indices_out, const float** values_out, uint32_t* count_out) {
    // ... writes to current slot, then advances with wrap-around
    g_sparse_buffer_idx = (g_sparse_buffer_idx + 1) % 16;
    return 1;
}
```

Affected buffers (all in `ffi/zvec_ffi.cc`):

| Buffer | Line | Type |
|--------|------|------|
| `g_pk_buf` | 1140 | Single slot |
| `g_string_buf` | 1157 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_buf` | 1181 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_fp64_buf` | 1182 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_int8_buf` | 1230 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_fp16_buf` | 1243 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_int16_buf` | 1280 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_binary32_buf` | 1293 | Single slot |
| `g_vector_binary64_buf` | 1306 | Single slot |
| `g_binary_buf` | 1356 | Single slot |
| `g_array_*_buf` | 1369-1445 | Single slot each |
| `g_names_buf` | 1506 | Single slot |
| `g_sparse_buffers` | 1262 | 16 slots (circular) |
| `g_sparse_fp16_buffers` | 1332 | 16 slots (circular) |

## Attack Scenario

In the current PHP FFI usage model, there is no practical exploit path because `FFI::string()` copies data immediately. However, if a C++ direct consumer calls:

```cpp
const char* pk = zvec_doc_get_pk(doc1);
const char* name = zvec_doc_get_string(doc2, "name");  // overwrites g_pk_buf
// pk now points to name's data — data corruption
```

This would only affect future C++ consumers not using FFI.

## Solution

Document the limitation in `zvec_ffi.h` and expand the sparse circular buffers from 16 to 256 slots for a larger safety margin. Do NOT change the single-slot buffers (that would be a breaking API change).

### Rationale

- **No impact on current PHP consumers**: `FFI::string()` copies data immediately, so the existing PHP bindings are safe
- **Minimal change**: Documenting the contract and expanding the most dangerous buffer (sparse circular at 16 slots) is sufficient
- **Least code**: Adding caller-allocated buffers (Option B) would be a breaking API change affecting every getter function — not justified for a non-exploitable issue in the current usage
- **No external dependencies**: Documentation is self-contained

```cpp
// In zvec_ffi.h — add documentation comment

/**
 * Pointer lifetimes:
 * - String/vector pointer return values are valid only until the next
 *   call to the same function from the same thread.
 * - Sparse vector results use a circular buffer of 256 slots.
 * - Callers MUST copy data before calling any other getter function.

**Background:**
Reflected cross-site scripting vulnerabilities arise when data is copied from a request and echoed into the application's immediate response in an unsafe way. An attacker can use the vulnerability to construct a request that, if issued by another application user, will cause JavaScript code supplied by the attacker to execute within the user's browser in the context of that user's session with the application. The attacker-supplied code can perform a wide variety of actions, such as stealing the victim's session token or login credentials, performing arbitrary actions on the victim's behalf, and logging their keystrokes. Users can be induced to issue the attacker's crafted request in various ways. For example, the attacker can send a victim a link containing a malicious URL in an email or instant message. They can submit the link to popular web sites that allow content authoring, for example in blog comments. And they can create an innocuous looking web site that causes anyone viewing it to make arbitrary cross-domain requests to the vulnerable application (using either the GET or the POST method). The security impact of cross-site scripting vulnerabilities is dependent upon the nature of the vulnerable application, the kinds of data and functionality that it contains, and the other applications that belong to the same domain and organization. If the application is used only to display non-sensitive public content, with no authentication or access control functionality, then a cross-site scripting flaw may be considered low risk. However, if the same application resides on a domain that can access cookies for other more security-critical applications, then the vulnerability could be used to attack those other applications, and so may be considered high risk. Similarly, if the organization that owns the application is a likely target for phishing attacks, then the vulnerability could be leveraged to lend credibility to such attacks, by injecting Trojan functionality into the vulnerable application and exploiting users' trust in the organization in order to capture credentials for other applications that it owns. In many kinds of application, such as those providing online banking functionality, cross-site scripting should always be considered high risk.

**Remediation:**
In most situations where user-controllable data is copied into application responses, cross-site scripting attacks can be prevented using two layers of defenses: Input should be validated as strictly as possible on arrival, given the kind of content that it is expected to contain. Vulnerability Details

Axios is a promise based HTTP client for the browser and Node.js. Prior to 1.15.0 and 0.31.0, Axios does not correctly handle hostname normalization when checking NO_PROXY rules. Requests to loopback addresses like localhost. (with a trailing dot) or [::1] (IPv6 literal) skip NO_PROXY matching and go through the configured proxy. This goes against what developers expect and lets attackers force requests through a proxy, even if NO_PROXY is set up to protect loopback or internal services. This issue leads to the possibility of proxy bypass and SSRF vulnerabilities allowing attackers to reach sensitive loopback or internal services despite the configured protections. This vulnerability is fixed in 1.15.0 and 0.31.0.
